article_text:
While accepting the Middleburg Film Festival Achievement in Acting Award this weekend, Léa Seydoux told the crowd that her parents sent her to summer camp in Middleburg. “The first time I came to the United States,” she said, “I flew on my own, and I was eight years old, and I didn’t speak a word of English, which is true. I knew how to say ‘yes,’ ‘no,’ and ‘sorry, I don’t understand.’ So it was it was difficult, but also rewarding. I discovered a new culture. I didn’t know then that I would become an actress, and that this would be my life: traveling, discovering new cultures, and exploring human nature.”

That has become the 41-year-old Seydoux’s hallmark, as she accompanied her Cannes breakout “Gentle Monster” ( Netflix ) to Middleburg with Austrian filmmaker Marie Kreutzer. Seydoux is in the running for the Best Actress Oscar.

Kreutzer grabbed the germ of an idea for the film from a 2020 newspaper article about pedophiles. “The article made it clear to me how close [to us] the perpetrators mostly are in most cases,” she said. “And that I must certainly also know not only victims of child sexual abuse but also perpetrators myself.”

When Seydoux first heard about the film from her agents, she was hesitant. As the mother of two children, “I was a bit scared of it,” she said. “I read the script, and I fell in love with the character. The script was so well-written, so intelligent, and that was it.”

In the film, when Lucy Weiss, a French pop singer living with her Austrian husband (Laurence Rupp) and young son in the country, finds out that her husband is accused of abusing children, “she’s in a state of shock,” said Seydoux. As the revelations about his behavior keep coming, “It’s a shock after another shock. It’s all these contradictions. This is what I loved about the character. It’s through her perspective that the story unfolds. It’s not through the victim’s perspective, not through the traitor’s perspective, but through her. I was able to bring a lot of different emotions that are not explainable with words.”

Seydoux is often silently reacting. “I used my facial expressions,” she said. “I try to to express internalized emotions with my body and my face. That was extremely interesting for me as an actor.”

Kreutzer structured a script that starts off with an intimate relationship with the husband, then evolves as Lucy finds out one thing after another, terrified that she might discover that her son was a victim of her husband’s predatory behavior. “After doing research and learning more about the subject,” said Kreutzer, “I became aware that I had had so many stereotypes in my head about pedophile criminals, so I really wanted to show a man and a couple that could feel like friends to an audience, a guy who would never have any suspicions of that kind. I like to get the audience to like them, to feel close to them. And then when all of this unfolds, also being in Lucy’s shoes and not wanting this to be true, and hoping for her and hoping for him that it’s not true, and that there will be some explanation, because that’s very human. When it comes to someone we know and have trusted, it’s much harder to accept that they have done awful things.”

Added Seydoux, “When it’s someone we know, that’s way harder to to accept because everyone has different sides to them, and also monstrous people have likable sides.”

Seydoux had to speak three languages on this film: English, French, and German. “Of course the German language is difficult in the pronunciation,” she said. “I found it difficult to play the emotions with the language you don’t speak. But then I had to be, emotionally speaking, in a strong emotion. There was a word that I struggled to pronounce, and at some point I remember that I burst into tears. Lucy can’t really express herself, and she doesn’t speak the language either, and so she’s even more isolated.”

The great Catherine Deneuve, who plays Lucy’s mother, points out that she’s supposed to be in the city, not in the country, because she’s a performer. “Yes,” said Seydoux. “The hardest part for me was the piano and the technical aspects. We spent some time in Vienna with Marie and a piano teacher who helped me. I had to press the right keys. The singing is my voice. I’m proud of it, and I’ve always loved singing. So that was for me also a dream come true.”

After 20 years in the business, Seydoux has learned many lessons, but none as heart-wrenching as shooting Abdellatif Kechiche’s “Blue Is the Warmest Color,” which won the Palme d’Or in 2013 for the director as well as his two actresses, Seydoux and Adele Excharpoulos.

“That was thirteen years ago,” Seydoux said, “at the time before the #MeToo movement. I’ve spoken already a lot about how disrespectful the director had been with us. We shot for six months, and we just discovered the movie in Cannes. The scenes were graphic, let’s say. So I discovered them during Cannes, which is absolutely crazy, and I didn’t have any approval on these scenes. We won the Palme d’Or, which makes us in a way co-writers of the film, which was true. True, because there was a lot of improvisations, and the story is based on both of us.”

It was after that award that things got complicated when Seydoux started to speak out about “the bad conditions,” she said. “The producers came to me and said, ‘You better shut your mouth, because if you want to be nominated for something, if you want to do the award season, you better stop.’ And I said ‘no, I want to explain how mistreated we’ve been on this film,’ and I didn’t say half of what happened. Really, it was horrible. And so I got fired. They fired me for promotion. It was difficult because then the director started to bully me. He said that if I was speaking, it’s because I come from this privileged family.”

Seydoux has never revealed the promo firing before. At a Golden Globes Q&A, Seydoux was challenged by some of the HFPA members, who said she was speaking out because of her family. “This was so humiliating,” said Seydoux. “Even now I could cry, but I’m not doing it. But I burst into tears and it was hard.”

“Since “Blue,” Seydoux has worked steadily with directors in France and Hollywood, from Wes Anderson (“The Grand Budapest Hotel”) and Woody Allen (“Midnight in Paris”) to Mia Hansen-Løve (“One Fine Morning”).

After #MeToo, her director has not returned to his previous station in international cinema. And Seydoux demanded final approval on any scenes involving her naked body. “When you work hand in hand with a director,” she said, “as I as I did with Marie, she showed me the scenes. I need to have the approval of that because it’s so intimate.”
excerpt_original: Marie Kreutzer's "Gentle Monster" is yet another example of how Seydoux explores the dark side of the human psyche. It could land her an Oscar nomination.

article_text:
‘The weirdos were taking over!’ Tate Britain relives the 1990s – in pictures

A new exhibition curated by Edward Enniful looks back on the thrilling decade before smartphones, when art, music and fashion came together with a bang

Thu 8 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT

Domenique, London, 29 September, 1998 by Juergen Teller

The 90s: Art and Fashion exhibition runs at Tate Britain, London, from 8 October 2026 to 14 February 2027 . Texts by Edward Enninful and Alex Farquharson

Pendragon at The Fridge, 1999, by David Swindells

Chopper Mark II, 2001, by Koto Bolofo

Northampton, 1997, by Elaine Constantine

Metalheadz, 1995-1996, by Eddie Otchere

Naomi Campbell, 1994, by Ellen von Unwerth

Susanne and Lutz, White Dress, Army Skirt, 1993, by Wolfgang Tillmans

Rosemary Ferguson, 1993, by Corinne Day

Vauxhall Bridge, from the series Pissing Women, 1995, by Sophy Rickett

Young Pink Kate, London, 1998, by Juergen Teller

Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show, 1998, by Eileen Perrier

Alek Wek, 1996, by Mark Mattock

Explore more on these topics

editorial_title_zh: “我们现在是一家人了”：比尔·皮克特牛仔竞技大赛——摄影随笔
editorial_excerpt_zh: 多年来，克洛伊·凯尔鲁（Chloe Kerleroux）一直在拍摄美国南部的非裔美国牛仔社群。她的作品主要聚焦于小径骑行（trail rides）：将马匹、音乐、舞蹈、家庭和社群生活汇聚在一起的大型聚会。今年，她将镜头转向了牛仔竞技……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在西部片和流行文化中广泛描绘的牛仔形象，长期以来几乎全是白人。然而，黑人牛仔在美国西部历史中占据着重要地位。南北战争和废除奴隶制之后，许多非裔美国人在牧场以及向西驱赶牛群的大道上找到了工作。历史学家估计，到19世纪末，大约四分之一的牛仔是黑人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "塑造这段历史的黑人人物中包括比尔·皮克特（Bill Pickett）。他于1870年出生于得克萨斯州，成为他那个时代最著名的黑人牛仔和竞技表演者之一，尤其以普及“斗牛摔”（bulldogging）而闻名，这一技巧最终催生了现代猛牛摔跤。", "links": [{"text": "Bill Pickett", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/ng-interactive/2024/may/19/black-cowboys-cowgirls-rodeos"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a407bd0a481f4acbe6ae3c77a58facdac3de9f42/0_0_7330_4929/master/7330.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "一名戴着牛仔帽的男子在竞技场里骑马", "caption": "国歌奏响后，“头号通缉犯”（Outlaws Most Wanted）成员乔希（Josh）伴随着动感的嘻哈音乐在竞技场中策马驰骋，队友们在一旁为他呐喊助威。2026年8月2日，摄于佐治亚州亚特兰大附近的康yers（Conyers）的比尔·皮克特邀请赛牛仔竞技大赛上。", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9f7908403f44c350716dce75fb5522712e186ff4/0_0_7728_5152/master/7728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "一群戴着牛仔帽的男子互相开玩笑", "caption": "在牛仔竞技大赛的后台，“头号通缉犯”的成员们开着玩笑，并向其他骑手发起轻松的挑战，其中一些骑手为了参赛历经长途跋涉。", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他的名字是由推广人卢·瓦森（Lu Vason）在创立比尔·皮克特邀请赛牛仔竞技大赛时选定的。1977年，瓦森参加了夏延边境节（Cheyenne Frontier Days），对竞技场中缺乏黑人牛仔的现象深感震惊。他的研究将他带到了丹佛的黑人美国西部博物馆（Black American West Museum），在那里他发现了皮克特的故事以及非裔美国人在美国西部的历史。1984年，他创立了一项牛仔竞技大赛，旨在为黑人男女牛仔提供一个平台，并让这种传统获得更多关注。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "40多年后，这一使命依然是比尔·皮克特邀请赛牛仔竞技大赛的核心。它兼具体育竞技、奇观盛会以及传承历史文化的空间属性，其2026年的巡回赛于2月至10月横跨美国，途经孟菲斯、亚特兰大、奥克兰和洛杉矶等地。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年，我决定在亚特兰大加入巡回赛。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/77dac485df3bc3853c0ffa53454e3ba935ab1508/0_0_7728_5152/master/7728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "一个带着三个戴牛仔帽的小孩子的男子骑在马上", "caption": "一个骑马的家庭正等待进入牛仔竞技赛场，这体现了代代相传的牛仔文化的跨代际特质。2026年8月1日", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在那里，我第一次见到了我在出行前一直在联系的受访者。他经营着钻石切口牧场（Diamondcut Ranch），在那里他从事并训练马匹，一个更为广泛的骑手社群也围绕着该牧场形成。正是在那里，我遇到了“头号通缉犯”，这是一支在比尔·皮克特大赛中竞技的“野马骑手”（bronc riders）团队。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "组织者允许我进入隔离栏后方，条件是我必须跟他们待在一起。我发现自己身处竞技场正后方的区域，骑手们在这里等待轮次并准备装备。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "音乐无处不在。骑手们开着玩笑，互相鼓励，彼此打气。随着他们的轮次临近，能量和肾上腺素不断上升，直到每位骑手都必须脱离这种集体的兴奋，专注于竞技场中等待他的那短短几秒钟。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c0342ddb8e4062be0b85b7586e637926f2fc81bb/643_0_6442_5152/master/6442.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "夜色中戴着牛仔帽的男子", "caption": "拉奇德·罗宾斯（Rachied Robins），人称“姜戈”（Django），是“头号通缉犯”野马骑行团队的成员，他成了我在比尔·皮克特邀请赛牛仔竞技大赛期间的主要联系人，也是讲述该团体故事的核心之声。2026年1月8日", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中一位名叫拉奇德·罗宾斯（人称“姜戈”）的成员将“头号通缉犯”描述为一群加勒比海男子，其中一些人有着艰难的背景，因对马匹的热爱而聚在一起。他说，有些人“在这个马的世界里找到了避难所”。随着时间推移，他们的纽带变得更加深厚：“我们现在是一家人了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "姜戈在佛罗里达州基西米（Kissimmee）长大，周围环绕着牛仔竞技文化。他最初从事的是骑公牛，但在一次公牛踩踏他的面部后更换了项目。他现在参加牧场野马骑行（ranch bronc riding）比赛，并笑着形容自己是个“肾上腺素瘾君子”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但在肾上腺素的背后，也存在着恐惧。在他骑上马之前，危险的想法以及各种“万一”在他的脑海中闪过。随后，他必须想办法清空大脑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e85111002152c3812ec5312cebd645b10fa41d42/0_0_6530_4414/master/6530.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "一群戴着牛仔帽的男人和男孩指向远方", "caption": "比尔·皮克特牛仔竞技大赛上的“头号通缉犯”野马骑行团队", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“你只需清空大脑，一切交给上帝。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他必须信任自己的技术并坚持过8秒钟。即便骑行结束，危险也并未解除：姜戈告诉我，从马上下来可能是最危险的时刻之一。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "参赛还有经济层面。姜戈告诉我，比尔·皮克特并不是提供最高奖金的牛仔竞技大赛之一：他说，在他参加的4月活动中，骑手最多可以赢得约$1,500（£1,135），而在某些其他牛仔竞技大赛中奖金高达$10,000。但金钱只是权衡因素的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这不仅关乎金钱，还关乎你的名声、尊重和排名。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，比尔·皮克特牛仔竞技大会最令我触动的地方，或许发生在竞技本身之外。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a11f430efc106c98549db2bece215fbe6265620a/0_0_7725_4765/master/7725.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "骑马的人们在竞技场外等候", "caption": "在竞技开始前的日落时分，骑手们神情肃穆地等待入场，他们将帽子贴在胸口，此时正清唱着《星条旗》", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在赛事开始前，现场清唱起《星条旗》。人们将帽子放在胸口，骑手们肃立不动，看台和竞技场上一片寂静。我记得当时自己起了一身鸡皮疙瘩，眼里泛起泪花。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后，几乎没有过渡，气氛骤然转变，肾上腺素瞬间飙升。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伴随着强劲的嘻哈音乐，所有骑手一同进入竞技场。音量放大，马匹鱼贯而入，人群欢呼、鼓掌并跳起舞来。转瞬之间，气氛便从肃穆的静止转变为几乎要爆炸般的能量。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种对比浓缩了我对比尔·皮克特牛仔竞技大会的大部分感受。历史和记忆是活动的核心，但它们并非凝固在过去。它们与嘻哈、时尚、竞技以及极具当代的黑人牛仔文化共存。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/42a2ae2b2683708bfff46961dc194be95320b181/20_0_6220_3919/master/6220.jpg?width=465&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "一名牛仔站在竞技场边缘，看台上的观众正为他欢呼", "caption": "在比尔·皮克特竞技大会上，一名牛仔在完成骑乘后沿着竞技场边缘走动，看台上的观众为他欢呼", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
T he image of the cowboy widely portrayed in westerns and popular culture has long been almost exclusively white. Yet Black cowboys hold an important place in the history of the American west. After the civil war and the abolition of slavery, many African Americans found work on ranches and on the great cattle drives westward. By the late 19th century, historians estimate about one in four cowboys were Black.

Among the Black figures who shaped this history was Bill Pickett . Born in Texas in 1870, he became one of the most celebrated Black cowboys and rodeo performers of his time, known in particular for popularising bulldogging, which would eventually give rise to modern steer wrestling.

His name was chosen by the promoter Lu Vason when he created the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. In 1977, Vason attended Cheyenne frontier days and was struck by the absence of Black cowboys in the arena. His research led him to the Black American West Museum in Denver, where he discovered the story of Pickett and the history of African Americans in the American west. In 1984, he created a rodeo designed to give Black cowboys and cowgirls a platform and bring greater visibility to this heritage.

More than 40 years later, that mission remains at the heart of the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. Part sporting competition, part spectacle and part space for passing on history and culture, its 2026 tour crosses the US from February to October, with stops including Memphis, Atlanta, Oakland and Los Angeles.

This year, I decided to join the tour in Atlanta.

While there, I met for the first time a contact I had been speaking with before my trip. He runs Diamondcut Ranch, where he works with and trains horses, and around which a wider community of riders has formed. It was there that I met the Outlaws Most Wanted, a team of “bronc riders” competing at the Bill Pickett.

The organisers allowed me behind the barriers on the condition that I stayed with them. I found myself in the space just behind the arena, where the riders wait for their turn and prepare their equipment.

Music is everywhere. The riders joke around, encourage one another and build each other up. The energy and adrenaline rise as their turn approaches, until each rider has to move away from that collective excitement and focus on the few seconds waiting for him in the arena.

One of them, Rachied Robins, AKA Django, describes the Outlaws Most Wanted as a group of Caribbean men, some of whom have come from difficult backgrounds, brought together by their love of horses. Some, he says, found “refuge in this horse world”. Over time, their bonds grew stronger: “We’re in a brotherhood now.”

Django grew up in Kissimmee, Florida, surrounded by rodeo culture. He started out in bull riding before changing disciplines after a bull stomped on his face. He now competes in ranch bronc riding and laughingly describes himself as an “adrenaline junkie”.

But behind the adrenaline, there is also fear. Before he gets on the horse, thoughts of the danger and all the “what ifs” run through his mind. Then he has to find a way to clear his head.

“You just gotta clear your mind and leave it in God’s hands.”

He has to trust his technique and make it through eight seconds. And even once the ride is over, the danger is not: Django tells me that getting off the horse can be one of the most dangerous moments.

There is also a financial side to competing. Django tells me that the Bill Pickett is not among the rodeos offering the largest purses: at the April event he competed in, he says a rider could win up to about $1,500 (£1,135), compared with as much as $10,000 at some other rodeos. But money is only part of what is at stake.

“It’s not just the money, but also your name, the respect, ranking.”

What struck me most about the Bill Pickett, however, perhaps happens beyond the competition itself.

Before the events begin, The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella. Hats are placed over hearts, the riders stand still, and silence falls across the stands and the arena. I remember getting goosebumps and tears in my eyes.

Then, almost without transition, the atmosphere shifts completely and the adrenaline takes over.

All the riders enter the arena to a powerful hip-hop track. The volume rises, the horses come in, and the crowd shouts, applauds and dances. Within moments, the atmosphere moves from solemn stillness to an almost explosive energy.

That contrast captures much of what I felt at the Bill Pickett. History and memory are central to the event, but they are not frozen in the past. They coexist with hip-hop, fashion, competition and a deeply contemporary Black cowboy culture.

The audience is very much part of the spectacle. Western shirts, cowboy hats and boots fill the stands: people come to watch the rodeo, but also to gather, dance, show their style and celebrate a shared culture. Throughout the event, the announcers return again and again to the history of Black cowboys and the values the Bill Pickett seeks to pass on. That history is not confined to a few lines in a programme: it is an integral part of the event.

When I ask Django what the Bill Pickett means to him, he tells me that it is about more than just rodeo: “Bill Pickett means a lot to me personally. Not just because it’s a rodeo, but because it’s a platform for us minorities to come together.”

He talks about being able to show what they can do “as a group, as a unit”, but also about having a place where he can be himself and where he feels at home.

The Outlaws Most Wanted do not compete only at Black rodeos. Django tells me they compete wherever they have the opportunity and rejects the idea that these events are a form of separation. For him, they are above all about making a heritage visible: “We just want to bring out our heritage and bring out our history and show that we are part of this history, and this is part of our history.”

It is also about passing something on. From trail rides to rodeos, horses create a space around which families, friendships and communities are formed. For some members of the Outlaws Most Wanted, this world has even become a refuge.

When I ask Django what he hopes the young people in the stands take away from watching him ride, he does not talk about becoming a cowboy or winning competitions. Above all, he hopes to show them that another path is possible: “Do something safe, do something legal, get out the streets, keep your mind right, don’t be another statistic.”

More than a century after Black cowboys helped shape the history of the American west while remaining largely absent from its popular image, the Bill Pickett offers a space where this heritage does not belong only to the past: it continues to be lived, passed on and reinvented.

article_text:
Danny Trejo was excited to play the good guy.

His son, filmmaker Gilbert Trejo, remembers being with the 82-year-old actor when his agent pitched “ Pawn Shop ” a few weeks before filming began. The movie would follow a Mexican American store owner trying to keep the peace amid protests and escalating violence. After a career spent playing convicts and criminals, the opportunity was appealing to Trejo.

“Oh, cool. I’m playing a good guy,” Gilbert recalled his father saying.

The people behind the indie project proved more controversial. Produced by Ben Shapiro ’s The Daily Wire and Bonfire Legend, the pro-ICE action movie has since drawn protests and questions about why a beloved performer known for supporting immigrants would participate.

Danny’s agent, Gloria Hinojosa, told IndieWire that Trejo didn’t personally know that Shapiro or The Daily Wire was involved when he accepted the role. Gilbert said his father thought he was playing a sympathetic character, and further described his own fears that walking away or criticizing the project could expose his dad to litigation the actor can’t afford.

Asked whether Danny felt empowered to turn down work, Gilbert pointed to his prolific output. With a sprawling filmography including “Heat,” “Desperado,” “From Dusk Till Dawn,” “Spy Kids,” and “Machete,” Trejo has amassed nearly 500 credits across film, television, video games, and music .

“I think his IMDb attests to the fact that no, he hasn’t been saying no,” Gilbert said. “He’s like most of us in this country. People are not turning down work.”

Gilbert said he sees his father almost every day but that he was not involved in negotiating “Pawn Shop.” He hasn’t reviewed his dad’s contract for the film , either. Nevertheless, Trejo’s predicament echos a question raised by IndieWire’s earlier reporting : What did the people hired to make this film know before taking the job, and what choices did they have after it started?

“Danny didn’t hear about Ben Shapiro’s or The Daily Wire’s involvement until a couple weeks ago,” Hinojosa confirmed to IndieWire in an October 13 email. “He was not familiar with nor had he ever heard of either before.” Trejo’s agent also directed IndieWire to her client’s recent social media statement.

“I am a proud Mexican who has always been and always will be a supporter of my community,” Danny wrote. “I am also obviously, pro immigrant. I am not pro ice.”

“I know where I come from and I know our struggles,” Trejo continued. “I am an actor. My job is to tell a story.” Neither The Daily Wire nor Bonfire Legend responded to IndieWire’s request for comment on the actor’s involvement, and Hinojosa’s email response did not address the claim that her client could not criticize the film publicly. “Pawn Shop” reportedly follows a federal immigration agent who takes shelter in a Minneapolis pawn shop amid civil unrest. Trejo plays the owner, a Mexican American military veteran.

Harvey Keitel, Henry Thomas, and others also star. The film, shot in Livingston, Montana, prompted protests and public safety complaints earlier this month. City officials temporarily suspended the production’s shooting permit before reinstating it with additional restrictions, and The Daily Wire announced on October 9 that filming had wrapped .

A screenplay draft, previously verified by a crew member and reviewed by IndieWire, includes a sequence resembling the fatal shooting of Renée Good by an ICE officer in Minneapolis earlier this year. In those pages, a protester strikes an ICE officer with her car before being shot by his partner, and the officer subsequently dies. No agents died in the real-life incident, and whether Good’s car ever posed a threat to her killer, Jonathan Ross, remains widely disputed .

“No one reached out to my dad and said, ‘Hey, we want to make some pro-ICE propaganda,’” Gilbert said, when pressed on the content of the “Pawn Shop” script as he understood it.

Not recognizing the producers and not understanding the movie are different things, to be sure. And neither Hinojosa nor Gilbert specified for IndieWire what was in the script Danny received or when he learned more about its overall portrayal of ICE. “Pawn Shop” was also not his first Daily Wire job.

Trejo previously voiced a character on Adam Carolla’s DailyWire+ animated comedy “Mr. Birchum,” whose December 2023 announcement also named Bonfire Legend’s Dallas Sonnier as a producer and Shapiro as an executive producer. Gilbert described that assignment as a casual acquaintance asking his father to voice a cartoon, without Danny meaningfully appreciating the companies involved.

Gilbert doubted his father would have recognized Shapiro walking around on set. He also believes he alerted Hinojosa, Danny’s agent of decades, to the political implications of the partnership amid the “Pawn Shop” controversy. He said her reaction suggested the team hadn’t fully understood them.

“It’s really hard to believe when you know everything that’s going on online that other people don’t,” Gilbert said, describing his father’s attention as living closer to home. For Danny, Hollywood is part of the local economy: a place to earn a living through assignments that often follow a familiar daily routine and steady yearly cycle.

“He looks at Hollywood like it’s a factory. It’s a factory that makes movies,” Gilbert said. “My dad thinks about Hollywood like it’s Detroit.”

Trejo’s challenge for much of his career has been getting more roles, and now there are fewer for everyone. A formerly incarcerated Mexican American actor, Danny built his legacy from parts that often reduced men with his background to a threat. “And he’s one of the very few Mexican men, especially of his generation, who have been able to turn getting cast as a convict, getting cast as a gangster, inmate number three, inmate number four, into goodwill and good faith,” Gilbert said.

Acting gave Danny a wider audience for the community work he had been doing for years, his son said. At prisons, schools, and recovery meetings, people recognize a Trejo character first and then listen to the man’s own story. On the day of our interview, Gilbert said, Danny recorded a voiceover and distributed socks to homeless people. He keeps them in his car just for that purpose.

“He feels like this career was given to him in order for him to help people, so he wants to keep working,” Gilbert said. “He just wants to work. That’s what he wants to do.”

Trejo’s financial troubles are public record. After he filed for personal Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2023, a judge approved a five-year plan to repay roughly $3 million in tax debts, including through the sale of one of his two Los Angeles homes, Bloomberg Law reported . His restaurant businesses were outside the bankruptcy , but Trejo said in a court declaration that approximately 90 percent of his income for the tax years at issue came from acting. The Hollywood strikes further interrupted that cash flow.

An April 2025 interim case closure does not establish his remaining debt or available funds today. IndieWire contacted his bankruptcy attorney, Jeffrey S. Shinbrot, for clarification. Still, Gilbert fears his father could not afford a legal fight. “It’s like, yeah, if I’m Tom Cruise , sure, whatever,” he said. “You know what I mean? But if I’m a hardworking 82-year-old Mexican American man, that’s not the case.”

IndieWire has not reviewed Trejo’s contract and cannot establish what consequences he might have faced for walking away from “Pawn Shop.” SAG-AFTRA previously told IndieWire that productions are expected to give performers enough information to make informed decisions.

“Misleading a performer about the role may undermine the meeting of the minds required to form a binding contract,” a spokesperson said. (The union did not respond before publication to additional questions about Trejo’s circumstances or the production’s current signatory status.)

An anonymous “Pawn Shop” crew member interviewed for our earlier investigation said they accepted what was only described as a “fun action movie” without knowing its connection to The Daily Wire or Shapiro, too. The worker ultimately left the shoot over political and safety concerns.

Reached again after the claims about Trejo became public, the worker remained skeptical that the principal cast could have been so uninformed. They emphasized that, in the version of the script they saw, Trejo’s character was “ultimately helping the ICE agent,” but they also had no firsthand knowledge of the actor’s negotiations and did not stay for most of the filming.

“I don’t want to discredit what he’s saying, and I would like to believe that that is the truth,” they said.

Speaking out has brought its own complications for Gilbert, who wanted to explain his father’s position without making it harder for him to navigate. His initial explanation was intended for a smaller audience. On October 10, he posted an Instagram Close Friends story describing his father as “handcuffed to this stupid project.” It circulated in the press, and Gilbert said he would have phrased it differently had he expected his comments to be shared widely.

“I hate the idea that any of what I would have said would be used against him in any sort of litigious way,” he said. “I’m not saying that anger is the problem. I’m saying the problem is there’s so much to be angry about. It’s very difficult to say, ‘I’m mad, I’m angry over here,’ and to stop and go, ‘Wait, who does my anger benefit?’”

Explaining the fallout to his father has also meant explaining internet outrage. To show that disconnect, Gilbert recalled once asking Danny not to post photos of him on social media because commenters had mocked him for not looking tough enough to be Trejo’s son. His dad’s response, Gilbert said: “When you put something on there, they can say things back to you?”

“Fortunately, people believe in him, and he tells his story, and they know that he’s been through what he’s been through,” he continued. “Unfortunately, they expect him to think with their brain as well.”

There’s irony, Gilbert said, in realizing that his father has played rapists, drug dealers, and cartel members without audiences mistaking their beliefs for his own. But it was taking a turn as the so-called “good guy” that left Danny having to explain himself.

“He’s playing a game he always thought was checkers, and now it’s chess,” Gilbert said.

A likable and even heroic character can still serve a political argument. But the younger Trejo’s account at least offers an explanation for why his father took the job with Shapiro’s Daily Wire. And whatever Danny understood when he accepted “Pawn Shop,” the filmmakers are using his face to tell their story.
excerpt_original: Gilbert Trejo discusses the "Pawn Shop" backlash after his father’s agent told IndieWire the actor didn't know Ben Shapiro or The Daily Wire were involved when he accepted the role.

article_text:
James Gray’s Paper Tiger , starring Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson, and Miles Teller, will make its MENA premiere at the second Doha Film Festival in November.

It is among seven features unveiled by the Qatari festival on Monday for its Gala and Special Screenings lineup.

Further titles getting the red carpet treatment include Rami Kodeih’s Beirut-set thriller Furies , about two sisters who plot a bank heist to pay for medical treatment. It world premiered in the Venice Spotlight section in September.

Both titles were produced by Brazilian producer Rodrigo Teixeira under his RT Features banner, and were supported by the Film Committee at Media City Qatar as part of its concerted push into international film business, unveiled on the eve of the inaugural Doha Film Festival last year.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Teixeira was also joined on Furies by executive producers George Clooney and Grant Heslov under their Smokehouse Pictures banner.

The Gala lineup also features Australian director Jeffrey Walker’s family adventure Fing! ; Maiken Baird’s Toronto-selected Edward Said: Between Worlds and Bruno Dumont’s Red Rocks .

The Special Screenings selection includes Abderrahmane Sissako’s Artou , the first 360° immersive film by the Mauritanian-born Malian Timbuktu director, which was also backed by the Film Committee.

The work, which debuted in Venice’s Immersive competition, follows three sisters and three brothers on their journey from Europe to Mauritania to fulfill the last wish of their father to be laid to rest beside his father in his native village.

Other Special Screenings include Daniele Rugo’s Life Support , following international doctors working alongside local medical staff in Gaza in 2023; Ginevra Elkann drama The Roses of Marrakech and Ali El Arabi’s 52 Blue , about a reclusive young man’s journey from Kerala to Qatar in a bid to meet his idol Lionel Messi during the Qatar World Cup.

“Our Gala and Special Screenings will bring audiences together through films that move, surprise, and spark conversation,” said Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, CEO of Doha Film Institute (DFI) and Director of Doha Film Festival.

“From gripping dramas and timely documentaries to stories filled with humour, adventure and discovery, the selection celebrates the courage to question what we take for granted and find dignity and truth in the complexity of human experience.”

The Doha Film Festival expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period.

The Gala and Special Screenings titles join the previously announced International Competitio n as well as a selection of local productions .

The festival will unfold from November 19 to 27.

article_text:
My third week in Switzerland began with another trip to Zurich to listen to a talk on archives, memory and the role of artistic research in the context of the exhibition “A Kind of Paradise— Colonial-Era Photography in Contemporary Art” at Museum Rietberg. The talk was being held in a cool, almost subterranean space, inside the basement of the museum. As I walked down the staircase, I felt a strange mood settling over me.

The works featured in the group exhibition were connected by the thread of global histories of colonial exploitation. I watched the Black and Brown bodies displayed within the white cube, equally moved by the artists’ renditions and interventions, as well as appalled at the pain and cruelty of the enslaved and oppressed, whose inadvertent consumer, I too, had become, simply through the act of looking.

Installation view of Sasha Huber’s work, featuring stapled photographs of enslaved individuals commissioned by Swiss-American naturalist Louis Agassiz

In the work of Sammy Baloji, I found resonance between the exploitative mining history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the fate of my own hometown, Dhanbad, where the spectre of exploitative forces continues to haunt the everyday lives of labouring bodies.

From the Memoire series by Sammy Baloji, merging archival photographs from Union Minière du Haut-Katanga and present-day images of abandoned mining structures

I realised that this exhibition will continue to weigh on my mind, as I continue my research work, investigating postcolonial narratives, and building methodologies for critical writing that question the role of photography and art in the age of extractive capitalism.

Finally, the highlight of my third week in Switzerland was the Art in Conflict- Discussion series by Artas Foundation, where I was invited by my research coach to artistically document the event. The roundtable conversation format brought together artists, researchers, dancers, social workers, people from various backgrounds and practitioners of various disciplines. As I listened to the speakers and their practice, exploring the possibilities of space in peace-building, I found myself searching for the ways language shapes our relationship with space. The evening inspired a poem, and after having spent the last few years solely dedicated to non-fiction, this was a welcome change.

Art in Conflict- Discussion series by Artas Foundation

From colonial historical past to modern conflict regions, this week was spent ruminating on global crises and critical and creative responses to the world around us. The week ended with a visit to an exhibition dedicated to Swiss women photographers that posed some very relevant questions regarding the privileges and barriers that shape the lives of women who choose to express artistically, a circumstance that I am all too aware of in my own life as well.

At the entrance of Fotostiftung Schweiz

I am signing off this dispatch with a mind brimming with new ideas and a heart still missing home, but finally more in sync with the Swiss terrain.
